did_you_know.text: The verb 'וַיַּחֲרִימָהּ' refers to herem — a ban/devotion of a city, meaning it was devoted (often destroyed) rather than treated as ordinary spoil.
The verse contrasts Gibeon with Ai, noting Gibeon was larger; the phrase 'mighty warriors' indicates the city had trained fighters.
'Adoni‑Zedek' is a royal name including the title 'Adoni'; the kings he summons were rulers of Amorite city‑states in the hill country and Negev.
The five kings and their forces represent an alliance of city‑states opposing Gibeon—intercity coalitions were common in Canaan.
The men of Gibeon ran to Gilgal for aid; Gilgal served as Israel's camp and political‑military center after crossing the Jordan.
The text says Joshua and his troops came up suddenly from Gilgal at night—highlighting a rapid night march uncommon for many ancient armies.
The pursuit took the ascent of Beth‑Horon—this pass was a strategic route connecting the plain and the Judean highlands.
It says 'stones of hail' were hurled from heaven killing many; in ancient texts storms and hail are often depicted as divine weapons.
Joshua speaks to the LORD and asks that the sun stand still; the passage also cites the 'Book of the Upright', likely an older collection of songs or annals now lost.
The statement 'the LORD fought for Israel' emphasizes the biblical motif of God as warrior acting on behalf of the people.
Five kings fled and hid in a cave at Makkedah; Makkedah appears elsewhere in the Bible and its precise archaeological identification is debated.
His order to roll a stone to the cave mouth echoes the practice of sealing caves; having soldiers place their feet on the kings' necks was a gesture of humiliation and victory.
The kings were hung on trees until evening, then taken down and thrown into the cave; later law (Deuteronomy) forbids leaving bodies hanging overnight, and here they were removed the same day.
Joshua's victories cover 'the hill country, the Negev, the lowlands and the Shephelah'—the text says the kings and their lands were taken 'at one time', suggesting a single decisive campaign.
